title: Organise and record the transportation, handling, moving and loading of livestock, game and agricultural products

lessons.title: Handling, moving and loading
lessons.html:
Working with animal behaviour

At this level you are the person in the pens and on the ramp. Good handling protects the animals, the meat and you.

  • Animals see almost all around them but have a blind spot directly behind. Do not stand there.
  • Move into the flight zone to make animals move, step back to stop them.
  • Animals follow each other. Move small groups, not one at a time.
  • Keep calm and quiet. Use flags or paddles. Never twist tails, hit or kick animals.
  • For game, follow the capture team's instructions. Keep quiet, stay out of sight, and never enter a boma alone.

Moving agricultural products

Handle produce carefully: bruised fruit and torn bags lose money. Lift with your legs, not your back, and use trolleys or forklifts for heavy loads. Keep products dry, shaded and away from fuel, fertiliser and chemicals.

Loading and unloading safely

  1. Check the vehicle is clean and safe, with partitions, no sharp edges and a good floor.
  2. Line the ramp up with the truck so there is no gap.
  3. Check each animal is fit to travel. Leave behind sick, injured, weak or heavily pregnant animals and tell your supervisor.
  4. Load to the density your supervisor gives from the code of practice.
  5. Close each partition gate behind the group.
  6. At the destination, unload quietly, give water and check for injuries.

Never climb into a compartment with cattle on board or put your arm through the sides of a moving truck. Cruel handling or transport is an offence under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.

lessons.title: Identification, weighing, organising transport and documents
lessons.html:
Permanent identification

The Animal Identification Act 6 of 2002 requires owners to mark their livestock with a registered identification mark. Permanent methods include:

  • Branding with a hot or freeze brand, used on cattle.
  • Tattooing in the ear, common on sheep, goats and pigs.
  • Microchips, used for horses, game and stud animals.

Ear tags help with management but can be lost, so they are not enough on their own. Branding and tattooing must be done by trained people with the animal properly restrained, to keep pain and injury to a minimum.

Weighing

Check that the scale is zeroed and working before you start. Weigh animals one at a time or in groups as instructed. Write down the animal number, weight, date and your name straight away. Weigh bags and bins of produce the same way and keep the tickets.

Organising transport

Before the truck arrives, make sure:

  • The number of animals or the amount of product is ready and sorted.
  • The vehicle booked is the right type and size.
  • The driver knows the address, route and arrival time.
  • Water and handling equipment are ready, and the ramp is safe.

Documents

DocumentWhy
Stock removal documentRequired under the Stock Theft Act 57 of 1959 when transporting livestock
Veterinary movement permitFor animals from or into disease control areas
Game transport permitFrom the provincial conservation authority
Weight tickets, delivery noteProof of what was sent

Check the numbers on the documents match what is on the truck. Give copies to the driver and keep a copy on the farm.

Key points

  • Use the flight zone and herd behaviour; never hit or twist tails.
  • Do not load unfit animals; report them to your supervisor.
  • Brands, tattoos and microchips are permanent identification under the Animal Identification Act 6 of 2002.
  • Zero the scale and record weights straight away.
  • Check that documents match the load before the truck leaves.
